name: Pūtanā
summary: Child-killing female being sent by Kaṃsa to poison the infant Kṛṣṇa with her breast-milk; he sucks out her life. The Harivaṃśa calls her a bird (śakunī) and Kaṃsa's nurse, the Bhāgavata a rākṣasī.
details: HV (CE) 50.20–24 describes Pūtanā as a terrifying bird (śakunī) who suckles the child at midnight and is struck down by him; HV 45.6 names her a daughter of Bali. ViP 5.5.7–11 has her offer the poisoned breast at night and fall dead. BhP 10.6 expands the scene (beautiful disguise, her huge corpse, its fragrant smoke on cremation) and makes her death a liberation (pūtanā-mokṣa, 10.6.44). Pūtanā is also the name of a child-afflicting female 'seizer' (graha) in medical and Purāṇic lists (e.g. BhP 10.6.27–28; Agni 298–299).

name: The rāsa dance (rāsa-līlā)
summary: On autumn nights Kṛṣṇa sports and dances with the cowherd women of Vraja. The Harivaṃśa gives a short erotic description; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa adds his disappearance, the gopīs' search by his footprints and the circular rāsa dance; the Bhāgavata expands it into five chapters (the rāsa-pañcādhyāyī) with the flute, the 'Gopī-gīta' and Kṛṣṇa multiplied between each pair of women.

ViP 5.13.14–62: Kṛṣṇa's song draws the gopīs; he vanishes; they imitate his deeds and trace his footprints and those of a favoured companion (5.13.31–40); he returns and forms the rāsa-maṇḍala holding each gopī by the hand (5.13.47–55). BhP 10.29–33: the flute (10.29), the disappearance (10.29.48), searching and the footprints of a favoured gopī (10.30.24–31), the Gopī-gīta (10.31), the reunion (10.32), and the dance in which Kṛṣṇa stands between every two gopīs (10.33.3), followed by Parīkṣit's question on its propriety (10.33.26–37).

summary: A wonder-working jewel passes from Satrājit (or Prasena) to Prasena, who is killed by a lion; the bear-king Jāmbavān kills the lion. name: Kṛṣṇa's killing of Naraka is commemorated on Naraka Caturdaśī / Dīpāvalī
summary: In much of western and southern India the day before (or the first day of) Dīpāvalī is Naraka Caturdaśī, observed as the day Kṛṣṇa (or Satyabhāmā) killed Naraka. details: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa (5.29) and Bhāgavata (10.59) give no festival rubric. Other regional explanations of Dīpāvalī (Rāma's return, Bali's annual visit, Lakṣmī worship) coexist; Kane surveys the medieval nibandha sources for the rites of the day.

The Purāṇic versions elaborate in different directions: the Matsya (129–140) makes Maya the hero of a long war; the Liṅga (1.71–72) and Śiva (2.5.1–12) say Viṣṇu first destroyed the asuras' dharma — in the Śiva Purāṇa by creating a shaven-headed teacher of a 'Jina' doctrine (2.5.4–5); the Bhāgavata (7.10.53–70) and Matsya (136.63–65) make Viṣṇu drink the nectar pond that revived the dead asuras (as a cow in BhP, as a bull in Matsya).
